title: TFSA Basics
summary: CONTRIBUTE → GROW TAX-FREE → WITHDRAW → ROOM RETURNS JAN 1
subtitle: Tax-Free Savings Account. It sounds like a plain savings account with a nice tax perk attached. It is much more than that.

blocks.text: Tax-Free Savings Account. It sounds like a plain savings account with a nice tax perk attached.
It’s much more flexible than that. A TFSA can hold stocks, bonds, funds and cash, not just a savings balance earning a little interest. And the growth inside it is free of Canadian tax for life.
The name is accurate. It’s also the reason a lot of Canadians underuse one of the best tools they have.
Let your savings grow for decades without handing a share to the tax bill.
blocks.detail: Knowing how TFSA room builds and comes back lets you use the account fully without a costly penalty.
blocks.extra: Section 04 shows the one timing rule that trips people up.

sections.title: The core idea, in one paragraph

blocks.text: You put in money that has already been taxed. Unlike an RRSP, there’s no deduction going in. But once it’s inside, everything that happens next is tax-free: growth, interest, dividends and every withdrawal, no matter how large the account grows.
That’s the whole idea, simple to describe. The details that trip people up are all about room and timing.

Two limits on “tax-free.” Dividends from U.S. stocks usually have 15% held back by the U.S., and a TFSA can’t get that back. And if you trade so often that the CRA sees it as a business, the profits can be taxed. For long-term saving, neither one gets in the way.

sections.title: Contribution room: what it is, and how it builds

blocks.text: Every year you’re 18 or older and a resident of Canada, you get new TFSA room. For 2026, that’s $7,000.
Room builds whether or not you open an account. It builds whether or not you have any income. Unlike an RRSP, a TFSA doesn’t care what you earned.

Room also carries forward. Never contributed, and eligible since the TFSA started in 2009? Your total room in 2026 is $109,000. Miss a year, or several, and that room waits for you. It doesn’t expire, and it doesn’t shrink.
TFSA room in 2026

items.title: Total room since 2009
items.text: $109,000 — if you were 18 or older in 2009 and have never contributed.

items.title: Unused room
items.text: Never expires — it carries forward to future years.

items.title: Room and income
items.text: Not linked — you get room even with no income.

items.title: “If I don’t use my TFSA room this year, I lose it.”
items.text: The opposite is true. Unused room carries forward forever. Someone who has never contributed still has all the room they’ve built up since they turned 18, or since 2009, whichever came later.

sections.title: Withdrawals: easy to take out, easy to mess up putting back

blocks.text: Take money out of a TFSA, and it’s yours: no tax, no penalty, no questions asked.
Here’s the part that catches people. The amount you take out is added back to your room, but not right away, and not that same year. It comes back on January 1 of the next year.
Take out $5,000 in June, and you might think you can put it back in August. You can’t, unless you already have other unused room. That $5,000 doesn’t return as room until next January 1.
CREDIT PULSE SPOTLIGHT: THE MISTAKE THAT COSTS PEOPLE REAL MONEY

This is the most common TFSA mistake, and it happens to people who are otherwise careful with money. Someone maxes out their TFSA. Mid-year, they take out a chunk for an emergency or a big purchase. A few months later, feeling flush, they put the same amount back, not knowing the room hasn’t returned yet. That’s an over-contribution, and the CRA charges 1% of the excess for every month it stays in. The fix: before you put back anything you took out this year, work out your room yourself.

Don’t trust the room figure in your CRA account mid-year. The CRA updates it once a year, in the spring, after banks report the year before. It doesn’t show what you put in or took out this year. To find your real room, start from the amount the CRA shows on January 1, then subtract every dollar you’ve put into any TFSA since then. Withdrawals from this year don’t count until next January.

sections.title: TFSA or RRSP — the question everyone asks eventually

blocks.text: Both are excellent tools, built for different moments.
An RRSP gives you a deduction now, and you pay tax later, when you take the money out. That’s usually in retirement, when your income and tax shelf are often lower.
A TFSA gives you no deduction now, but you never pay tax on it again: not on the growth and not on withdrawals.

A rough rule of thumb: if you’re on a low shelf now, a TFSA often makes more sense, since the RRSP deduction isn’t saving you much. If you’re on a high shelf, the RRSP deduction is doing real work and may come first. A TFSA also has a quiet bonus: withdrawals don’t count as income, so they don’t shrink benefits like Old Age Security or the Guaranteed Income Supplement later. Many Canadians use both and lean one way or the other depending on the year.

items.title: “A TFSA is only useful for short-term savings, like an emergency fund.”
items.text: That’s one good use, but far from the only one. A TFSA can hold long-term investments, like stocks, ETFs and mutual funds, and let decades of growth compound tax-free. Treating it only as a savings account leaves a much bigger tool on the table.

items.title: I know my real TFSA room: the CRA’s January 1 figure, minus what I’ve put in this year.
If I withdrew money this year, I know it won’t count as available room again until next January 1.
I understand a TFSA can hold investments, not just cash sitting at a low interest rate.
I’ve thought about whether a TFSA or an RRSP fits my situation better this year, or whether both make sense.

blocks.text: Owen’s expensive August
paragraphs: Owen drove a delivery van in Kelowna and was proud of one thing above all: he had maxed out his TFSA every year since he opened it. In June, he took out $15,000 to redo his kitchen, which was exactly the kind of thing the account was for.
In August, a $15,000 bonus landed. Owen grinned. He would put it straight back and the TFSA would look the way it had before the renovation.

He paused with the transfer ready. A coworker had once mentioned a rule about TFSA withdrawals, but Owen couldn’t remember what it was. He logged into his CRA account and saw plenty of room listed. That settled it. He hit Transfer.

The next spring, a letter arrived from the CRA. The room in his account hadn’t counted anything from that year. His withdrawn $15,000 wouldn’t come back as room until January 1, and he’d had no other room left. For the five months the money sat there, the CRA charged 1% a month on the excess: $750.

Owen sat at his new kitchen table, staring at the letter. He could have paid it and moved on. Instead, he asked the CRA to waive the penalty, explaining that it was an honest mistake and that he had already taken the extra money out. The CRA can cancel a penalty in cases like his, but it isn’t guaranteed.

He paid the $750 while he waited for an answer. Now Owen keeps a simple note on his phone: the January room figure, minus every deposit he makes. He checks it every time, before he touches the transfer button.

blocks.text: CREDIT PULSE SPOTLIGHT: NAME A SUCCESSOR HOLDER, NOT JUST A BENEFICIARY

If you have a spouse or common-law partner, name them as your TFSA’s successor holder, not just its beneficiary, where your province allows it. A successor holder takes over the account itself when you die. It stays a TFSA, keeps growing tax-free and uses none of their own room. A beneficiary gets the money tax-free, but the account closes. A spouse can often still move it into their own TFSA, but only with extra forms and a deadline. In Quebec, this choice is usually made in your will. Check your TFSA paperwork for the word “successor.” It’s usually one form.

A TFSA lets your money grow and come out tax-free, with no deduction going in and no tax after. Room builds every year whatever your income, and it never expires. But a withdrawal doesn’t restore your room until January 1 of the next year, and putting money back too soon is the most common, and costly, TFSA mistake.
Track your own room, and the TFSA rewards you for decades.
blocks.detail: A two-line note of what you put in this year protects you from penalties the CRA’s figure won’t warn you about.
blocks.extra: Section 08 walks you through your own TFSA check-in.

items.title: Find the room the CRA showed for January 1 this year, then subtract everything you’ve put into any TFSA since then.
If you took money out of your TFSA this year, write down the date and amount, so you know when that room comes back.
If your TFSA is mostly cash, think about whether it should hold longer-term investments. A licensed adviser can help if you’re unsure.

blocks.text: Worksheet: your TFSA check-in

Answer guidance: if your room is a guess, working it out is the most valuable five minutes in this lesson. Do it before you put in another dollar this year. If you made a withdrawal this year, mark next January 1 on your calendar as the day that room returns. If your TFSA is all cash, that’s not wrong, but it may be worth learning what else it could hold.

items.title: Contribution room
items.text: The amount you may put into your TFSA. It builds up every year.

items.title: Over-contribution
items.text: Putting in more than your room, which triggers a 1% monthly tax on the excess.

items.title: Qualified investment
items.text: The kinds of assets a TFSA can hold: cash, stocks, bonds, funds and more.

items.title: Non-resident
items.text: Someone who has moved out of Canada. Room stops building, and new contributions bring their own penalty.
